date.note: First printed in 1796 (at Slavuta) by Shneur Zalman of Liady, the Alter Rebbe. The book is titled Likutei Amarim ('a collection of sayings') and is called Tanya from its opening Hebrew word (tanya, 'it has been taught'); its first part is also titled Sefer shel Beinonim ('the Book of the Intermediate Man / of the Intermediates'). The digitized Hebrew and English text on Sefaria is the Kehot Publication Society edition.

summary: The Tanya (Likutei Amarim), first printed in 1796, is the foundational text of Chabad Hasidism, written by Shneur Zalman of Liady, the Alter Rebbe. Its first part, Sefer shel Beinonim ('the Book of the Intermediate Man'), sets out on Chabad's account the doctrine of the two souls of every Jew, an animal soul and a divine soul that is 'truly a part of God above', and holds up the beinoni, the 'intermediate' person who masters thought, speech, and deed but not the desire itself, as the attainable spiritual ideal in place of the tzaddik. It grounds the intellectualist ChaBaD path, the acronym of Chochmah, Binah, and Da'at (wisdom, understanding, and knowledge), by which sustained contemplation is taught to generate love and awe of God and cleaving to Him (devekut), and it opens from the oath of Niddah 30b, 'Be righteous and be not wicked... in your own eyes regard yourself as if you were wicked.'
description:
The Tanya is the systematic work of Hasidic thought composed by Shneur Zalman of Liady (1745-1812), the Alter Rebbe and founder of the Chabad (Lubavitch) school, and first printed in 1796. It is titled Likutei Amarim ('a collection of sayings') and is known as the Tanya from its opening Hebrew word, tanya ('it has been taught'); its principal and best-known first part bears the further title Sefer shel Beinonim, 'the Book of the Intermediate Man'. Within Chabad it is studied as the authoritative written statement of the school's teaching, and the account that follows presents its doctrines as the work's own attributed teaching rather than as claims the editor affirms or denies.

Part I, the Sefer shel Beinonim, opens (chapter 1) from a rabbinic passage: the oath said to be administered to the soul before birth (Niddah 30b), 'Be righteous and be not wicked; and even if the whole world tells you that you are righteous, in your own eyes regard yourself as if you were wicked.' Shneur Zalman notes at once the tension between this oath and the Mishnaic counsel of Avot ('be not wicked in your own estimation'), and between regarding oneself as wicked and the joy in which God is to be served, and he sets the resolution of this tension as a governing problem of the book, working from the Talmud's five types (a righteous man who prospers, a righteous man who suffers, a wicked man who prospers, a wicked man who suffers, and a beinoni, an intermediate person). On this teaching the beinoni is not one whose deeds are half meritorious and half sinful, but the person who never actually sins in thought, speech, or deed while the desire to sin is not extinguished in him; the beinoni, and not the tzaddik (in whom the animal soul is transformed) nor the rasha (the wicked), is presented as the level that every person can attain, and the book is named for him.

The doctrinal core of Part I is the teaching of the two souls. Chapter 2 states that 'the second soul of a Jew is truly a part of God above', derived, on an analogy the text marks as such, from the divine 'thought and wisdom'; this divine soul is set against the animal or vital soul that animates the body and is the seat of the self-centred desires. Chabad's distinctive intellectualism is grounded here: the text glosses ChaBaD as an acronym of chochmah (wisdom), binah (understanding), and daat (knowledge), the first three of the ten sefirot, and (chapter 3) sets out the ten faculties of the soul 'corresponding to the supernal ten sefirot', dividing the soul 'in two, sechel (intellect) and middot (emotional attributes)', the three intellectual powers being the 'mothers' and source of the seven emotional attributes their 'offspring'. On this account the disciplined path to the love and awe of God, and to devekut (cleaving to Him), runs through the intellect: sustained contemplation (in the mind's chochmah, binah, and daat) of the greatness of God is taught to generate and govern the emotions of the heart, rather than the emotions being aroused directly. Chapter 2 further grounds the system in the Kabbalah, invoking Moses Cordovero's Pardes Rimonim and 'the Kabbalah of the Arizal' (Isaac Luria), the 'contractions' of the light of Ein Sof through the vessels of Chabad in the world of Atzilut, so that the Tanya presents itself as a continuation of Lurianic theosophy turned toward the inner life of the mind.

The Tanya as printed comprises further parts beyond the Sefer shel Beinonim, among them Shaar ha-Yichud veha-Emunah ('the Gate of Unity and Faith'), Iggeret ha-Teshuvah ('the Letter of Repentance'), Iggeret ha-Kodesh ('the Holy Letter'), and Kuntres Acharon ('the Final Treatise'); this entry describes chiefly Part I, whose opening chapters carry the load-bearing doctrines named above. The book became the foundational text of Chabad and is studied and, in the movement, memorized within it as the authoritative statement of its doctrine; it is presented here on the tradition's own terms as that statement, with its teachings of the two souls, the beinoni, and the intellectualist path attributed to the work and its author and not adjudicated by the editor.
editorial_notes: This entry presents the Tanya (Likutei Amarim) on Judaism's own terms as the foundational text of Chabad Hasidism, written by Shneur Zalman of Liady (the Alter Rebbe) and first printed in 1796 (neutrality #1, #4, #6). Its doctrines, the two souls (the divine soul 'truly a part of God above' and the animal soul), the beinoni as the attainable ideal versus the tzaddik and the rasha, and the intellectualist ChaBaD path (Chochmah-Binah-Da'at) by which contemplation generates emotion and devekut, are stated throughout as the WORK'S OWN ATTRIBUTED teaching ('on this teaching', 'on this account', 'presents its doctrines as the work's own attributed teaching'), DESCRIBED and not affirmed or denied by the editor. The Chabad/Chagat distinction is not drawn as a ranking here; the intellectualist path is described, not judged superior to the affective piety of other Hasidism. Sources triangulate three lenses per neutrality #8-#9: (a) the PRIMARY text itself, open and auditable on Sefaria (Kehot Publication Society Hebrew and English, both CC-BY-NC), Part I chapters 1-3 READ LINE-BY-LINE; (b) academic monographs on the school and its founder, Naftali Loewenthal, Communicating the Infinite: The Emergence of the Habad School (Chicago, 1990), and Roman A. Foxbrunner, Habad: The Hasidism of R. Shneur Zalman of Lyady (Alabama, 1992); and (c) a contemporary Jewish scholar on-topic, Rachel Elior, The Paradoxical Ascent to God: The Kabbalistic Theosophy of Habad Hasidism (SUNY, 1993). No encyclopedias (no Encyclopaedia Judaica, no YIVO Encyclopedia, no Chabad.org, no My Jewish Learning), no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE / HONESTY: the Tanya (Likutei Amarim) on Sefaria is rated HIGH because Part I chapters 1-3 were READ line-by-line via the open Sefaria text API and the load-bearing lines were confirmed VERBATIM: chapter 1 opens from the oath (Niddah 30b), 'Be righteous and be not wicked; and even if the whole world tells you that you are righteous, in your own eyes regard yourself as if you were wicked', with the Talmud's five types (righteous who prospers/suffers, wicked who prospers/suffers, and the beinoni); chapter 2, 'The second soul of a Jew is truly a part of God above', grounded in Cordovero's Pardes and 'the Kabbalah of the Arizal', 'the clothing of the light of the En Sof'; chapter 3, the soul's ten faculties 'corresponding to the supernal ten sefirot', 'divided in two, sechel (intellect) and middot (emotional attributes)', with the intellect comprising 'chochmah (wisdom), binah (understanding), and daat (knowledge) (chabad)'. The Sefaria English is the Kehot Publication Society translation, and the ChaBaD acronym gloss quoted from the shneur-zalman entry ('an acronym formed of the initial letters... chochmah, binah, and daat') reflects the Kehot glosses read on those chapters; the acronym itself (chabad = chochmah, binah, daat) is stated verbatim in chapter 3 as read. The three monographs (Loewenthal, Foxbrunner, Elior) are MEDIUM, verified to exist and be on-topic via publisher, distributor, and Internet Archive records, not read line-by-line; Loewenthal and Foxbrunner carry the same medium rating they hold in shneur-zalman.json.
